## Report: Chalmers, "Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness"

**1. The question, frozen.**
The paper answers several questions. The title and opening make the central one: *What explains conscious experience — why and how does physical processing give rise to there being something it is like?* Range: any system, any modality; asked forward (what produces it), with a backward part (what we can tell from our own case and from reports). Frozen here. The paper's half-century diagnosis (Sections 2–5) and its candidate theory (6–8) are tested together, since the theory leans on the diagnosis.

**2. The explanation in parts.**
P1 the easy/hard split; P2 functions are explained by mechanisms; P3 the explanatory gap (any specifiable physical process could occur without experience); P4 the need for an "extra ingredient"; P5 experience taken as fundamental, with new basic laws; P6 structural coherence; P7 organizational invariance; P8 double-aspect information; P9 naturalistic dualism's shape; P10 rival ingredients (quantum, nonalgorithmic, new neurophysiology) ruled out.

**3. Part by part.**
Never added up.

| Part | Mark | Why, and where it came from |
|---|---|---|
| P1 easy/hard split | **Held** | Swap "experience" back to "awareness" and the paper becomes Crick, Koch, Baars — which it shows fails the job. Built, with the target in view. |
| P2 functions → mechanisms | **Borrowed** | Rests on the standard account of reductive explanation in the sciences. Not tested here. |
| P3 explanatory gap | **Held if** | Held only by "a physical process could conceivably occur without experience." That job is itself in doubt: P7 later says the experience-free case is impossible. Name the doubt. Built from conceivability. |
| P4 extra ingredient | **Held if** | Same doubtful job as P3. Remove P3 and nothing asks for an extra ingredient. |
| P5 experience as fundamental | **Fixed** | The owner sets it ("I suggest…"), and openly says it does not explain why there is experience. Not tested; said out loud. Good. |
| P6 structural coherence | **Held** | Works on colour space and visual geometry: remove it and those matchings go unexplained. But it is untested on the case that would break it — awareness without experience. |
| P7 organizational invariance | **Held if** | Held by "we would notice a change in experience." That premise is the coherence principle again, so the thought experiment partly assumes what it argues. Built. |
| P8 double-aspect information | **Loose** | No answer to which information is phenomenal; the author calls it underdetermined. Nothing on the change list could replace or confirm it. Asserted. |
| P9 naturalistic dualism | **Borrowed** | Its shape (fundamental entities plus laws) rests on the Maxwell/mass analogy. Name the rival: panpsychism. |
| P10 rival ingredients dismissed | **Held** | One shared form — "more dynamics gives only dynamics" — does the work. Caution below. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**
*Flip.* Had reductive methods succeeded, the paper would be wrong, not resourceful. Passing.
*Direction.* Poke the physical side (swap a neuron for a chip) and the theory says experience moves; poke experience (imagine red and green inverted) and it says processing stays. Correct direction. But P8 flattens this: two aspects of one information space leave no cause and no effect, so the reverse test stops biting.
*Hidden in the starting points?* Partly. The hard problem's engine, "physical explanation entails only structure and function," risks making "physical accounts cannot yield experience" true by definition of "physical." The readable version is P3's conceivability claim, which is why P3 must carry the weight — and P7 undercuts it. That is the paper's central pull: **P3 and P7 pull against each other.** The line drawn is "logically possible, nomologically impossible." What would show the line is wrong: any case where conceivability tracks real possibility, or any physical account richer than structure and dynamics. The paper concedes the gap without drawing this line's defence.
*Catch-alls.* "Psychophysical principles" is a catch-all: whatever functions you explain, a bridging law absorbs the rest. The method allows one only with a gauge — something measurable that would show it swallowing a job. None is offered. P8 is admitted to be underdetermined; the thermostat question is left open. **No gauge.**
*P10 as catch-all.* The dismissal has a form that would rule out any future physical account by construction. Held, but it needs the same gauge: name what a successful physical account would have to do that it currently cannot.
*Change list leaves out.* Which information is phenomenal; why experience is not uniform if it is fundamental; where awareness and experience part. The last is left out openly, which is honest, but it is exactly the case the theory needs.
*Jobs' provenance.* P1, P3, P4 are the author's own. Expect fit; the fit proves little.
*Provenance.* P1, P3, P5, P7 built; P6 fitted to existing colour and geometry work; P8, P9 asserted; P2 borrowed.
*Rivals.* Against panpsychism, nothing on the list separates "all information is phenomenal" from "some is." At this level they are one explanation; Chalmers half-says so.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.**
One job: a case where awareness and experience come apart (global availability with no experience, or the reverse). That single case would either break P6 or force it into a firmer claim. Second: a gauge for P8 — a measurement deciding which information carries a phenomenal aspect.

**6. What this does not show.**
Hard to vary is not true. The negative half (P1–P4, P10) is far tighter than the positive half (P5–P9). A loose positive half does not make the diagnosis wrong.

**7. One next step.**
Write down, before looking, one finding that would count against P6 — then go looking for it.
